COE Board of Earth Sciences, University of California, Santa Cruz Paleomagnetic and geologic investigations in Eocene volcanic rocks of the southwest Washington Coast Range demonstrate a close relationship between tectonic rotations and the local structural ge- ology. The allochthonous middle Eocene submarine basalt basement of the Crescent Formation consists of several fault-bounded structural domains up to 30 km across that are characterized by different amounts of clockwise rotation (20 ø to perhaps as much as 65 ø ) when compared to the Eocene reference pole for North America. Structural analysis shows the differential rotations postdate middle Eocene folding of the Crescent Formation

characterized by different amounts of clockwise rotation (20 ø to perhaps as much as 65 ø ) when compared to the Eocene reference pole for North America. Structural analysis shows the differential rotations postdate middle Eocene folding of the Crescent Formation against the continental margin and predate the unconformably overly- ing upper Eocene Goble Volcanics, which are rotated about 23 ø and do not show the same domains of rotation as the underlying Crescent Formation. Post-Goble rotations may be accommodated by a fault pattern very similar to that expected for areas caught in a simple dextral shear couple along transcurrent faults. Major north-northwest trending faults with several kilometers of dextral dis

Thirty-five to 100% of the observed post-late Eocene rotations could have occurred by this shear rotation mechanism. Other paleomagnetic study areas in the Coast Range and western Cascades have a similar fault geometry and may also have undergone significant shear rotations. Long-term northward oblique subduction of the Farallon plate beneath the Coast Range throughout most of the Tertiary could have been the driving force for the shear rotations and could explain the rapid eastward decrease in rotation away from the continental margin. Shear rotations could eliminate many of the structural and stratigraphic difficulties associated with models involving rotation of large, rigid plates. 1. Thirty-five to 100% of the observed post-late Eocene rotations could have occurred by this shear rotation mechanism. Other paleomagnetic study areas in the Coast Range and western Cascades have a similar fault geometry and may also have undergone significant shear rotations. Long-term northward oblique subduction of the Farallon plate beneath the Coast Range throughout most of the Tertiary could have been the driving force for the shear rotations and could explain the rapid eastward decrease in rotation away from the continental margin. Shear rotations could eliminate many of the structural and stratigraphic difficulties associated with models involving rotation of large, rigid plates. 1. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: ney Department of Geological Sciences, The University of Michigan, Ann Arbor Abstract. A Middle/Late Silurian paleomag- netic pole has been obtained from reefal lime- stones in north central Indiana. Eleven of 25 collected sites yielded well clustered character- istic directions after stepwise alternating field demagnetization. One additional site gave the same characteristic direction after great circle analysis. These 12 site-level directions were used to calculate the mean paleomagnetic pole. Reef flank beds dip steeply (about 380 ) away from reef centers. Field and petrographic studies demonstrate that part of this dip is a primary depositional dip and that part is due to a tilt caused by early postdepositional differ- ential compact ion of under lying mudstone beds. Present attitudes of geopetal surfaces indicate that the postdepositional component of the obser- ved bedding dip is about 120 . A 120 tilt cor- rection to paleomagnetic directions from oppo- sitely dipping flank beds brings the mean directions into significantly better agreement, indicating that the magnetization was acquired early. The presence of both normal and reversed polarities also suggests early acquisition of the characteristic remanence. The mean of the site paleomagnetic poles (with sites from steeply inclined flank beds corrected for 120 of tilt) is 16.8øN, 124.9øE (K=74, A95--5.1ø), in good agreement with the Middle Silurian Rose Hill pole for North America. METHODS The majority of samples collected were drilled using port- able rock drills and oriented using both magnetic and sun compasses [Embleton, 1979']. The cores were later sliced into specimens of nominal dimensions 2.5 cm diameter x 2.2 cm height, usually yielding two to four specimens per core. Mag- netizations of specimens were measured using an ScT Squid magnetometer or Digico flux gate magnetometers. The latter instruments were only used for magnetic moments greater than approximately 10 -5 emu (10 -8 A m-). Demagnetization of specimens was performed with a three- axis tumbling alternating field (af) device (similar to that de- scribed by Roy et al. [1972]) or less frequently with Schon- stedt GSD-1 af equipment. Most specimens were demagne- tized using a furnace and zero-field coils similar to those de- scribed by McElhinny et al. [1971]. Demagnetization trends from all demagnetized specimens have been examined with the aid of both stereo nets and orthogonal plots [-Zijderveld, 1967]. The Digico anisotropy delineator has been calibrated against a susceptibility bridge thus avoiding problems recently brought to light by Hrouda eta!. [-1983] and Veitch et al. [1983-]. EMBLETON Division of Mineral Physics, Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization, North Ryde, New South Wales, Australia A total of 446 oriented samples have been collected from an Archaean intrusion and the Fortescue Group volcanics and intrusions in the Pilbara and Hamersley regions of northwestern Australia. The paleomagnetism and rock magnetism of these samples have been investigated using susceptibility and hysteresis properties and both alternating field (af) and thermal demagnetization. The most consistent paleomagnetic results were achieved by first applying af demagnetization and then stepwise thermal demagnetization. Evidence of the effects of lightning are widespread which accounts for the efficacy of this particular demagnetization strategy. Application of the fold test has resulted in placing significant constraints on the acquisition ages of some of the magnetizations and their corresponding pole positions. METHODS The majority of samples collected were drilled using port- able rock drills and oriented using both magnetic and sun compasses [Embleton, 1979']. The cores were later sliced into specimens of nominal dimensions 2.5 cm diameter x 2.2 cm height, usually yielding two to four specimens per core. Mag- netizations of specimens were measured using an ScT Squid magnetometer or Digico flux gate magnetometers. The latter instruments were only used for magnetic moments greater than approximately 10 -5 emu (10 -8 A m-). Demagnetization of specimens was performed with a three- axis tumbling alternating field (af) device (similar to that de- scribed by Roy et al. [1972]) or less frequently with Schon- stedt GSD-1 af equipment. Most specimens were demagne- tized using a furnace and zero-field coils similar to those de- scribed by McElhinny et al. [1971]. Demagnetization trends from all demagnetized specimens have been examined with the aid of both stereo nets and orthogonal plots [-Zijderveld, 1967]. The Digico anisotropy delineator has been calibrated against a susceptibility bridge thus avoiding problems recently brought to light by Hrouda eta!. [-1983] and Veitch et al. [1983-]. The mag- nitude of the dip as determined from layering of plagioclase crystals has been estimated to be 45 ø (R. Horwitz, personal communication, 1984). The magnetizations of these units are weak (<20 x 10 -6 emu cm-3 or 20 mA m-) and as seen from demag- netization of the NRM (Figure 13) they are multicomponent. The 15 sites are spread over some 20 by 30 km, and the internal consistency of the site-mean directions indicates that differential tilting of parts of the massif has not occurred. In order to obtain a better resolution of the Ordovician geomagnetic field direction in the Armorican Massif, sampling and paleomagnetic measurements were initiated in 1981 with a collection from the Late Ordovician Thouars Massif, Vende province, France. Geological Setting and Sampling The southern part of the Armorican Massif has been the site of a Siluro-Devonian orogenic phase, called the Ligerian orogeny [Cogn, 1977], and a paired metamorphic belt has been documented for this area [Lefort, 1979; Peucat et al., 1978]. The high-pressure, low- temperature metamorphism of the Ile de Groix gave rise to a blueschist facies with one of the better known pre-Mesozoic occurrences of glauco- phane in the world [Carpenter and Civetta, 1976]. Immediately to the north of this paired metamorphic belt, the South Armorican Shear Zone (SASZ) is marked by ultra-mylonites and leuco- granitic intrusions of Hercynian age; the SASZ has been interpreted as a dextral megashear of Carboniferous age [Jegouzo, 1980; Berth et al., 1979]. This character- istic magnetization yields a mean direction with declination/inclination = 340o/-83 ø , with k = 27 and 9S=7 ø, based on 15 sites. The south paleo- pole is located at 34øN, 5øE. A partial magnet- ic overprint of Hercynian age is observed in sites close to the South Armorican Shear Zone. The 15 sites are spread over some 20 by 30 km, and the internal consistency of the site-mean directions indicates that differential tilting of parts of the massif has not occurred. Since it appears to be unlikely that the entire massif was tilted, we infer that the characteristic direction is primary and that the paleopole adequately represents the local magnetic field in the Late Ordovician. The paleopole for the Thouars Massif supports previously obtained results from other Ordovician rocks in Hercynian Europe, but it is the first result to pass modern reliability criteria. The high Ordo- vician paleolatitudes of the Armorican Massif, other areas in Hercynian Europe, and north- western Africa, indicate that Gondwana and Armorica were adjacent until Late Ordovician time. Low paleolatitudes for Late Devonian time suggest that Armorica underwent rapid northward motion, at a rate of about 10 cm/yr, during the Silurian and earliest Devonian. Armoric

Secondary magnetizations with similar orien- ations occur in the Devonian or Mississippian Taylor and Permian Reeve formations, about 125 km north of our northernmost sampling locality (Figure 1), in an area of more intense Nevadan deformation [Hannah and Verosub, 1980]. A third suite of samples (32 samples from six sites) was collected from the Sonora dike swarm, an extensive swarm of east-northeast striking diabase dikes that intrudes the metamorphosed Calaveras and Shoo Fly complexes and the Standard pluton east of the Sonora fault [Schweickert, 1981; Schweickert and Bogen, 1983]. Six dikes were sampled from a region extending approxi- mately 4.5 km north-south and 2 km east-west. The dikes are not noticeably foliated in hand sample or thin section but do show minor evidence of low-grade metamorphism such as rare sphene and leucoxene and minor chlorite and epidote. Plagioclase laths are probably albitized. One of the dikes sampled yielded 157-159 Ma K-Ar horn- blende ages [Sharp, 1980] and we assume that these ages approximate that of the swarm. The ages correspond to the Oxfordian Stage according to Armstrong [1978] and thus the Sonora dikes are approximately the same age as rocks in the upper part of the Logtown Ridge Formation. Ages of the Magnetizations The ages of the magnetizations are not bracketed completely but may be inferred with reasonble confidence. Component A is present in each of the three formations despite their dif- ferent ages. The magnetization postdates both brecciation of the Logtown Ridge pillow lavas and Nevadan folding of the Penon Blanco Formation. No younger metamorphic event is known to have affected the rocks at these localities and plutons of the Sierra Nevada batholith are 20-90 km distant from the sampling sites. If these plutons, which range in age from Late Jurassic to Late Cretaceous, were responsible for the remagnet- ization, then we would expect a distribution of Bogen et al.: Paleomagnetism of Jurassic Rocks 4633 poles streaked toward the Cretaceous reference pole, reflecting some 65 Ma over which the batholith developed. The Logtown Ridge Formation contains a component of higher coercivity than the Nevadan magnetization (component A), but this component is not reversed unless corrected for tilting due to the folding. If the higher-coercivity mag- netization directions were younger than component A, then major post-Jurassic displacement relative to North America would be implied, since this direction yields a pole position far from those of post-Jurassic North America (Table 2). zation is most likely the result of widespread re- rystallization of magnetite during low- greenschist facies metamorphism that accompanied the Nevadan orogeny. We suggest that the northwesterly magnetization may be a paleo- agneitc \"signature\" of the orogeny and an indicator of the areal extend of metamorphism. Steiner and Helsley [1975a,b] and Steiner [1980] have shown that numerous field reversals occurred during Late Jurassic time, but because each of their polarity intervals is much shorter than an age, we are unable to correlate the reversal(s) in our data with any specific reversal shown by them. It also is unlikely that our normal and reversed magnetizations represent consecutive polarity intervals, considering the frequency of field reversals during Late Jurassic time. Subvertical, bedded Mesozoic volcanic rocks metamorphosed to low greenschist facies predominate to the west, whereas Paleozoic metamorphic rocks of higher grade and greater structural complexity predominate to the east. The age of the Penon Blanco Formation is early Jurassic (180-200 Ma) based on radiometric dates [Morgan, 1976; Saleeby, 1982]. A third suite of samples (32 samples from six sites) was collected from the Sonora dike swarm, an extensive swarm of east-northeast striking diabase dikes that intrudes the metamorphosed Calaveras and Shoo Fly complexes and the Standard pluton east of the Sonora fault [Schweickert, 1981; Schweickert and Bogen, 1983]. Six dikes were sampled from a region extending approxi- mately 4.5 km north-south and 2 km east-west. The dikes are not noticeably foliated in hand sample or thin section but do show minor evidence of low-grade metamorphism such as rare sphene and leucoxene and minor chlorite and epidote. Plagioclase laths are probably albitized. One of the dikes sampled yielded 157-159 Ma K-Ar horn- blende ages [Sharp, 1980] and we assume that these ages approximate that of the swarm. The ages correspond to the Oxfordian Stage according to Armstrong [1978] and thus the Sonora dikes are approximately the same age as rocks in the upper part of the Logtown Ridge Formation. In most of these investigations, rotation was not suspected prior to the study because such deformation rarely has any clear-cut geologic expression other than aberrant paleodeclinations. Rotations about horizontal or subhorizontal axes (tilts), however, are not commonly deter- mined from paleomagnetic data. Other geologic markers, such as bedding, indicate tilts (due to folding or faulting), and these markers are usually used to correct paleomagnetic data or for the classic fold test [Graham, 1949] rather than to elucidate deformation. Where such markers are lacking, however, paleomagnetic data may be used to determine the extent of tectonic tilting [MacDonald, 1980]. Geissman et al. [1982], for example, used paleomagnetic data from Mesozoic basement rocks in the eastern Basin and Range province to document tilts greater than those shown by the stratified Cenozoic cover. Along continental margins, however, paleoinclination anomalies may be the result of either tilting due to folding or faulting or large-scale north-south transport. In addition, sequential rotations about multiple axes may well have occurred in regions of continental margin orogenesis where polyphase deformation is common [MacDonald, 98o]. The western belt of the Sierra Nevada (Figure 1) is one such orogenic region where both single- phase and polyphase deformation have occurred [Taliaferro, 1942; Clark, 1964, 1976; Schweickert et al., 1984]. A prominent fault system, con- sisting of the Melones and Sonora faults, tran- sects the region from north-northwest to south- southeast (Figure 1). The faults also divide the belt into a western part where deformation is relatively simple and has occurred largely during a single phase, and an eastern part, where deformation has been more complex with multiple phases locally. LITHOSTRATIGRAPHY OF THE TYPE NGORORA FORMATION The Kabarsero section of the Ngorora Formation (described by Bishop and Pickford [1975]) is composed of volcaniclastic and epiclastic sediments deposited on top of a weathered Tiim phonolite flow. It is well bedded on a millimeter to meter scale but displays substantial lateral facies variation, making lithostratigraphic correlations between isolated outcrops tenuous. Nearly all of the sedi- ments are reworked pyroclastic material, deposited in lakes and streams or on floodplains. Basement-derived clasts are extremely rare, comprising less than 0.1 vol % of the exposed strata. In the type area the formation is 420-460 m thick. At the base of the section the sediments are poorly sorted, volcaniclastic sandy siltstones and clays. Debris flows are common. The poorly sorted lower layers are overlain by cross-bedded tuffaceous fine sands and silts as well as an accretionary lapilli tuff. This unit is overlain by finely lam- inated clays and shales with minor channel-sand deposits. Superposed on these sediments is a sequence of clays interbedded with tuffaceous silts and sands. K-Ar isotopic systematics may be disturbed by a number of alteration processes affecting the parent/daughter ratios and/or the content of radiogenic argon. Loss of radiogenic argon is the most cited process which decreases the K-Ar age of a geologic sample. How- ever, diffusion rates of argon out of sanidine are too slow to allow escape of argon from the Kenya sanidines; on the basis of the thermal demagnetization behavior of the Ngorora specimens, the Kenya sediments have not experi- enced temperatures in excess of 150øC (Figure 2b). For this reason, we believe that the sanidine ages reported in Table 2 are reliable estimates of the eruption ages. section_candidates.excerpt: Neogene Tectonic Rotation of the San Gabriel Region, California, Suggested by Paleomagnetic Vectors RICHARD R. TERRES ! AND BRUCEP. LUYENDYK Department of Geological Sciences, University of California, Santa Barbara Previous paleomagnetic work in the western Transverse Ranges and the islands offshore of Cali- fornia has suggested that these regions have experienced large clockwise rotations since middle Miocene time. This study is aimed at testing how far east these rotations extend into the con- tinent. Neogene volcanic rocks from the region bounded by the San Gabriel and San Andreas faults were selected for paleomagnetic study. The sampled units are lavas from the late Oligocene to early Miocene continental Vasquez Formation, and water-laid tuff beds from the middle to late Miocene Mint Canyon Formation. These rocks possess a stable remanent magnetization which was acquired soon after deposition and is believed to be primary. Seventy-four lava flows from eleven locations in the Vasquez Formation were studied. The average direction for seven locations near the center of the study area suggests that this area has rotated a net clockwise amount of 37.1 ø __+ 12.2 ø since the early Miocene. There is no suggestion of north or south translation. A location west of the centra

studied. The average direction for seven locations near the center of the study area suggests that this area has rotated a net clockwise amount of 37.1 ø __+ 12.2 ø since the early Miocene. There is no suggestion of north or south translation. A location west of the central region is rotated almost 90 ø clockwise, although this is believed to be a local effect. Detailed magnetic stratigraphy at the western and central location can be correlated over 6 km. Locations in the east near the San Andreas fault yielded highly dispersed directions which can- not now be interpreted in terms of rotation. The mean paleomagnetic direction from six sites (four different beds) in the Mint Canyon formation west of the Vasquez study area is deflected in a counterclockwise sense by 16 ø + 30 ø. These data are consistent with a proposed model in which the San Gabriel region first was rotated clockwise 53 ø (37 ø + 16 ø) in the early Miocene and later rotated 16 ø counterclockwise as it slid northward into the leftward bend region of the San Andreas fault. The clockwise rotation is believed to be due to dextral shear within the Pacific-North Ameri- can plate shear zone; counterclockwise rotation in the Mojave region is believed to be responsible for the bend in the San Andreas fault. section_candidates.excerpt: Neogene Tectonic Rotation of the San Gabriel Region, California, Suggested by Paleomagnetic Vectors RICHARD R. TERRES ! AND BRUCEP. LUYENDYK Department of Geological Sciences, University of California, Santa Barbara Previous paleomagnetic work in the western Transverse Ranges and the islands offshore of Cali- fornia has suggested that these regions have experienced large clockwise rotations since middle Miocene time. This study is aimed at testing how far east these rotations extend into the con- tinent. Neogene volcanic rocks from the region bounded by the San Gabriel and San Andreas faults were selected for paleomagnetic study. The sampled units are lavas from the late Oligocene to early Miocene continental Vasquez Formation, and water-laid tuff beds from the middle to late Miocene Mint Canyon Formation. These rocks possess a stable remanent magnetization which was acquired soon after deposition and is believed to be primary. Seventy-four lava flows from eleven locations in the Vasquez Formation were studied. The average direction for seven locations near the center of the study area suggests that this area has rotated a net clockwise amount of 37.1 ø __+ 12.2 ø since the early Miocene. There is no suggestion of north or south translation. A location west of the centra

studied. The average direction for seven locations near the center of the study area suggests that this area has rotated a net clockwise amount of 37.1 ø __+ 12.2 ø since the early Miocene. There is no suggestion of north or south translation. A location west of the central region is rotated almost 90 ø clockwise, although this is believed to be a local effect. Detailed magnetic stratigraphy at the western and central location can be correlated over 6 km. Locations in the east near the San Andreas fault yielded highly dispersed directions which can- not now be interpreted in terms of rotation. The mean paleomagnetic direction from six sites (four different beds) in the Mint Canyon formation west of the Vasquez study area is deflected in a counterclockwise sense by 16 ø + 30 ø. These data are consistent with a proposed model in which the San Gabriel region first was rotated clockwise 53 ø (37 ø + 16 ø) in the early Miocene and later rotated 16 ø counterclockwise as it slid northward into the leftward bend region of the San Andreas fault. The clockwise rotation is believed to be due to dextral shear within the Pacific-North Ameri- can plate shear zone; counterclockwise rotation in the Mojave region is believed to be responsible for the bend in the San Andreas fault. section_candidates.excerpt: Neogene Tectonic Rotation of the San Gabriel Region, California, Suggested by Paleomagnetic Vectors RICHARD R. TERRES ! AND BRUCEP. LUYENDYK Department of Geological Sciences, University of California, Santa Barbara Previous paleomagnetic work in the western Transverse Ranges and the islands offshore of Cali- fornia has suggested that these regions have experienced large clockwise rotations since middle Miocene time. This study is aimed at testing how far east these rotations extend into the con- tinent. Neogene volcanic rocks from the region bounded by the San Gabriel and San Andreas faults were selected for paleomagnetic study. The sampled units are lavas from the late Oligocene to early Miocene continental Vasquez Formation, and water-laid tuff beds from the middle to late Miocene Mint Canyon Formation. These rocks possess a stable remanent magnetization which was acquired soon after deposition and is believed to be primary. Seventy-four lava flows from eleven locations in the Vasquez Formation were studied. The average direction for seven locations near the center of the study area suggests that this area has rotated a net clockwise amount of 37.1 ø __+ 12.2 ø since the early Miocene. There is no suggestion of north or south translation. A location west of the centra

studied. The average direction for seven locations near the center of the study area suggests that this area has rotated a net clockwise amount of 37.1 ø __+ 12.2 ø since the early Miocene. There is no suggestion of north or south translation. A location west of the central region is rotated almost 90 ø clockwise, although this is believed to be a local effect. Detailed magnetic stratigraphy at the western and central location can be correlated over 6 km. Locations in the east near the San Andreas fault yielded highly dispersed directions which can- not now be interpreted in terms of rotation. The mean paleomagnetic direction from six sites (four different beds) in the Mint Canyon formation west of the Vasquez study area is deflected in a counterclockwise sense by 16 ø + 30 ø. These data are consistent with a proposed model in which the San Gabriel region first was rotated clockwise 53 ø (37 ø + 16 ø) in the early Miocene and later rotated 16 ø counterclockwise as it slid northward into the leftward bend region of the San Andreas fault. The clockwise rotation is believed to be due to dextral shear within the Pacific-North Ameri- can plate shear zone; counterclockwise rotation in the Mojave region is believed to be responsible for the bend in the San Andreas fault. section_candidates.excerpt: Neogene Tectonic Rotation of the San Gabriel Region, California, Suggested by Paleomagnetic Vectors RICHARD R. TERRES ! AND BRUCEP. LUYENDYK Department of Geological Sciences, University of California, Santa Barbara Previous paleomagnetic work in the western Transverse Ranges and the islands offshore of Cali- fornia has suggested that these regions have experienced large clockwise rotations since middle Miocene time. This study is aimed at testing how far east these rotations extend into the con- tinent. Neogene volcanic rocks from the region bounded by the San Gabriel and San Andreas faults were selected for paleomagnetic study. The sampled units are lavas from the late Oligocene to early Miocene continental Vasquez Formation, and water-laid tuff beds from the middle to late Miocene Mint Canyon Formation. These rocks possess a stable remanent magnetization which was acquired soon after deposition and is believed to be primary. Seventy-four lava flows from eleven locations in the Vasquez Formation were studied. The average direction for seven locations near the center of the study area suggests that this area has rotated a net clockwise amount of 37.1 ø __+ 12.2 ø since the early Miocene. There is no suggestion of north or south translation. A location west of the centra

studied. The average direction for seven locations near the center of the study area suggests that this area has rotated a net clockwise amount of 37.1 ø __+ 12.2 ø since the early Miocene. There is no suggestion of north or south translation. A location west of the central region is rotated almost 90 ø clockwise, although this is believed to be a local effect. Detailed magnetic stratigraphy at the western and central location can be correlated over 6 km. Locations in the east near the San Andreas fault yielded highly dispersed directions which can- not now be interpreted in terms of rotation. The mean paleomagnetic direction from six sites (four different beds) in the Mint Canyon formation west of the Vasquez study area is deflected in a counterclockwise sense by 16 ø + 30 ø. These data are consistent with a proposed model in which the San Gabriel region first was rotated clockwise 53 ø (37 ø + 16 ø) in the early Miocene and later rotated 16 ø counterclockwise as it slid northward into the leftward bend region of the San Andreas fault. The clockwise rotation is believed to be due to dextral shear within the Pacific-North Ameri- can plate shear zone; counterclockwise rotation in the Mojave region is believed to be responsible for the bend in the San Andreas fault. section_candidates.excerpt: Neogene Tectonic Rotation of the San Gabriel Region, California, Suggested by Paleomagnetic Vectors RICHARD R. TERRES ! AND BRUCEP. LUYENDYK Department of Geological Sciences, University of California, Santa Barbara Previous paleomagnetic work in the western Transverse Ranges and the islands offshore of Cali- fornia has suggested that these regions have experienced large clockwise rotations since middle Miocene time. This study is aimed at testing how far east these rotations extend into the con- tinent. Neogene volcanic rocks from the region bounded by the San Gabriel and San Andreas faults were selected for paleomagnetic study. The sampled units are lavas from the late Oligocene to early Miocene continental Vasquez Formation, and water-laid tuff beds from the middle to late Miocene Mint Canyon Formation. These rocks possess a stable remanent magnetization which was acquired soon after deposition and is believed to be primary. Seventy-four lava flows from eleven locations in the Vasquez Formation were studied. The average direction for seven locations near the center of the study area suggests that this area has rotated a net clockwise amount of 37.1 ø __+ 12.2 ø since the early Miocene. There is no suggestion of north or south translation. A location west of the centra

studied. The average direction for seven locations near the center of the study area suggests that this area has rotated a net clockwise amount of 37.1 ø __+ 12.2 ø since the early Miocene. There is no suggestion of north or south translation. A location west of the central region is rotated almost 90 ø clockwise, although this is believed to be a local effect. Detailed magnetic stratigraphy at the western and central location can be correlated over 6 km. Locations in the east near the San Andreas fault yielded highly dispersed directions which can- not now be interpreted in terms of rotation. The mean paleomagnetic direction from six sites (four different beds) in the Mint Canyon formation west of the Vasquez study area is deflected in a counterclockwise sense by 16 ø + 30 ø. These data are consistent with a proposed model in which the San Gabriel region first was rotated clockwise 53 ø (37 ø + 16 ø) in the early Miocene and later rotated 16 ø counterclockwise as it slid northward into the leftward bend region of the San Andreas fault. The clockwise rotation is believed to be due to dextral shear within the Pacific-North Ameri- can plate shear zone; counterclockwise rotation in the Mojave region is believed to be responsible for the bend in the San Andreas fault. section_candidates.excerpt: Neogene Tectonic Rotation of the San Gabriel Region, California, Suggested by Paleomagnetic Vectors RICHARD R. TERRES ! AND BRUCEP. LUYENDYK Department of Geological Sciences, University of California, Santa Barbara Previous paleomagnetic work in the western Transverse Ranges and the islands offshore of Cali- fornia has suggested that these regions have experienced large clockwise rotations since middle Miocene time. This study is aimed at testing how far east these rotations extend into the con- tinent. Neogene volcanic rocks from the region bounded by the San Gabriel and San Andreas faults were selected for paleomagnetic study. The sampled units are lavas from the late Oligocene to early Miocene continental Vasquez Formation, and water-laid tuff beds from the middle to late Miocene Mint Canyon Formation. These rocks possess a stable remanent magnetization which was acquired soon after deposition and is believed to be primary. Seventy-four lava flows from eleven locations in the Vasquez Formation were studied. The average direction for seven locations near the center of the study area suggests that this area has rotated a net clockwise amount of 37.1 ø __+ 12.2 ø since the early Miocene. There is no suggestion of north or south translation. A location west of the centra

studied. The average direction for seven locations near the center of the study area suggests that this area has rotated a net clockwise amount of 37.1 ø __+ 12.2 ø since the early Miocene. There is no suggestion of north or south translation. A location west of the central region is rotated almost 90 ø clockwise, although this is believed to be a local effect. Detailed magnetic stratigraphy at the western and central location can be correlated over 6 km. Locations in the east near the San Andreas fault yielded highly dispersed directions which can- not now be interpreted in terms of rotation. The mean paleomagnetic direction from six sites (four different beds) in the Mint Canyon formation west of the Vasquez study area is deflected in a counterclockwise sense by 16 ø + 30 ø. These data are consistent with a proposed model in which the San Gabriel region first was rotated clockwise 53 ø (37 ø + 16 ø) in the early Miocene and later rotated 16 ø counterclockwise as it slid northward into the leftward bend region of the San Andreas fault. The clockwise rotation is believed to be due to dextral shear within the Pacific-North Ameri- can plate shear zone; counterclockwise rotation in the Mojave region is believed to be responsible for the bend in the San Andreas fault. LUYENDYK Department of Geological Science, University of California, Santa Barbara Geologic observations and previous paleomagnetic studies have suggested that the western Transverse Ranges arrived at their anomalous east-west orientation by clockwise tectonic rotation. A paleomagnetic study of the northern Channel Islands was undertaken, in order to test the extent of rotated areas and to develop constraints on tectonic models concerning the formation of the southern California Borderland. The islands of Anacapa, Santa Cruz, Santa Rosa, and San Miguel form an east-west trending chain and are considered part of the Transverse Range physiographic province. The remanent magnetization in the dolomite is carried by pseudo-single-domain (PSD) detrital magnetite, and was probably acquired within a few meters of the seafloor [Hornafius, 1984b]. Paleomagnetic measurements from Paleocene volcanic rocks of the region were first reported by Helsley [1970], who sampled the Cantwell Formation at two localities within Denali National Park. Although the age of the Cantwell is now considered to be Paleocene on the basis of isotopic ages and plant fossils, the formation's age was thought to be Early Cretaceous at the time of Helsley's study. These eruptions caused collapse of the roof of the chamber to form Long Valley caldera and produced the extensive deposits of Bishop Tuff that surround it. Almost immediately after caldera collapse, eruptions re- sumed on the caldera floor, resulting in the accumulation of thick rhyolite tuffs and the outpouring of hot, fluidal rhyolite flows. These early postcaldera rhyolites consist typically of aphyric to sparsely porphyritic obsidian, containing only a few percent phenocrysts of plagioclase, hypersthene, Fe-Ti oxides, and biotite (in decreasing abundance). Eruption of this early rhyolite persisted during a relatively short time span (< 100,000 years) between 0.73 and 0.62 m.y. ago. These erup- tions were accompanied by resurgent doming of the caldera floor which resulted in contemporaneous uplift and faulting of the early rhyolite tuffs and flows. As a consequence, the west central part of the caldera is now occupied by a broad, arched resurgent dome that is 10 km in diameter and 500 m high, and is transected by a 2-km-wide, complexly faulted, northwest- trending medial graben. During resurgence a caldera lake also was forming, so that the ri

resurgence a caldera lake also was forming, so that the rising dome formed an island within it. Continued rise of the dome eventually caused the lake to overflow the topographically low southeast caldera rim, re- sulting in downcutting of the Owens River Gorge and gradual draining of the lake. During the past 0.5 m.y. as the lake receded, eruptions were confined to the caldera moat peripheral to the resurgent dome. This moat rhyolite contrasts texturally and mineral- ogically with the early rhyolite in being coarsely prophyritic and typically containing large phenocrysts of plagioclase, sani- dine, quartz, hornblende, biotite, and Fe-Ti oxides (in decreas- ing abundance). It is also characteristically pumiceous and was apparently quite viscous, as domes and flows are usually thick, steep-sided, and of limited extent. The moat rhyolite erupted during three distinct episodes, each comprising four or five individual domes or flows with associated pyroclastics and each localized in a different sector of the caldera moat. The eruptive episode occurred at about 0.5 m.y. ago on the north flank of the resurgent dome, about 0.3 m.y. ago in the southeast moat, and about 0.1 m.y. ago in the west moat. The informal names given the rock units within the caldera by Bailey et al. [1976] are used throughout this report. section_candidates.excerpt: urvey, Menlo Park, California Paleomagnetic measurements and K-Ar age determinations on volcanic rocks from Long Valley caldera, California, have enabled further refinement of eruptive activity within this large silicic volcanic center. K-Ar age determinations show that postcaldera volcanic eruptions began 0.73 m.y. ago and continued periodically until about 50,000 years ago. The eruptions were not temporally random but tended to occur in distinct episodes separated by periods of quiescence. Volcanism in the western half of the caldera was particularly intense between 0.15 and 0.50 m.y. ago, when many units ranging in composition from basalt to rhyolite were erupted. An average of the virtual geomagnetic poles for 33 units from the caldera yields a paleomagnetic pole at 89.7øN, 138.4øE, (595 = 5.1ø), which is indistinguish- able from the earth's rotational axis. The ancient geomagnetic field dispersion about this mean pole is 16.0 ø , with upper and lower limits of 19.3 ø and 13.6 ø , respectively. section_candidates.excerpt: California The history of poleward motion of the Baja California peninsula is a subject of continuing geologic investigations, including paleomagnetic studies during the past decade. Geologic correlations seem not to necessitate northward movement, while paleomagnetic data suggest movement of 1000 km or more. We have made paleomagnetic measurements on Cretaceous and Eocene sedimentary rocks of San Miguel Island, California, which are western lithofacies of rocks cropping out on the Baja peninsula. A total of 97 drill cores taken from Upper Cretaceous turbidites, though weakly magnetized, were found to clean best in response to thermal demagnetization, revealing a characteristic remanence. The characteristic magnetization has an inclination 43.9 ø, declination of 24.0 ø, and an 9s of 3.9 ø. section_candidates.excerpt: California The history of poleward motion of the Baja California peninsula is a subject of continuing geologic investigations, including paleomagnetic studies during the past decade. Geologic correlations seem not to necessitate northward movement, while paleomagnetic data suggest movement of 1000 km or more. We have made paleomagnetic measurements on Cretaceous and Eocene sedimentary rocks of San Miguel Island, California, which are western lithofacies of rocks cropping out on the Baja peninsula. A total of 97 drill cores taken from Upper Cretaceous turbidites, though weakly magnetized, were found to clean best in response to thermal demagnetization, revealing a characteristic remanence. Rogers and Ragland interpret the significance of this chemistry to be that the Clarno formed on a thin continental margin having a crustal thickness of 20 to 30 km. However, andesitic volcanic rocks temporally equivalent to the upper part of the Clarno (42 m.y. and younger) crop out in south central Oregon and across central Nevada and Utah [Walker, 1963; Wells, 1979; Stewart et al., 1977]. ENGEBRETSON 2 The Clarno Formation, a mostly Eocene and partly early Oligocene sequence of andesitic lavas and volcaniclastic rocks, is the oldest Tertiary formation exposed in north central Oregon. Rcmanent mag- netization directions at 46 sites in the lavas provide a paleomagnetic pole at 84øN, 278øE with a 95% confidence cone of 7 ø . Comparison of this pole with the North American reference pole for Eocene time indicates that the Clarno Formation has rotated 16 ø clockwise with an uncertainty of 10 ø but has undergone no significant latitudinal displacement. Further comparison with paleomagnetic data from the Miocene Columbia River Basalt Group and Steens Basalt shows that large-scale block rotations in the eastern Columbia Embayment ceased sometime between 38 m.y. and 15 m.y. A paleogeographic recon- struction for 38 m.y. is offered which is consistent with the observed rotation of the Clarno and with the other paleomagnetic data from the Pacific Northwest, which are briefly reviewed. This reconstruction shows that it is possible to account for virtually all of the paleomagnet

uction for 38 m.y. is offered which is consistent with the observed rotation of the Clarno and with the other paleomagnetic data from the Pacific Northwest, which are briefly reviewed. This reconstruction shows that it is possible to account for virtually all of the paleomagnetically indicated rotations in pre-Miocene Tertiary rocks of the Pacific Northwest by an extensional tectonic model. As a consequence, only part of the rotations in the pre-Tertiary rocks of the eastern Columbia Embayment need to be the result of accretionary tectonics. The initiation of magmatism in the eastern Columbia Embayment that is represented by the Clarno Formation itself may have been contemporaneous with the beginning of crustal extension in the Pacific Northwest. Declinations of reversely magnetized (I = -45 ø to -75 ø) Sunshine Peak Tuff change from easterly (D = 93ø-130 ø) throughout most of the tuff to southerly (D = 195ø-207 ø) within the late eruptive phases. The postcollapse lava flows are also reversely magnetized, and their emplacement appears to have spanned resurgence of the caldera. Although paleomagnetic data do not provide absolute ages, as do radiometric tech- niques, in this case it was possible to estimate relative time based on models of magnetic secular variation and on reason- ably well-established records of polarity reversals of the earth's field. The individual units of the Sunshine Peak Tuff were studied primarily to determine whether their eruption and cooling occurred over long or short periods of time, rela- tive to directional changes of the earth's paleomagnetic field. Paleomagnetic data were also obtained to aid in determining the time of resurgence relative to emplacement of lava flows and to assess whether exposures of the resurgent intrusions are part of one large intrusive body, as implied by geological, geochemical, and geophysical data, or alternatively represent separate bodies having different intrusive and cooling histor- ies

Finally, we considered the idea that the magnetic polarities of the units related to the Lake City caldera might be used to estimate crudely the lifespan of the caldera. Samples were collected from 86 paleomagnetic sites from the islands of Luzon, Marinduque, Mindoro, Panay, Negros, Cebu, and Mindanao in the Philippine Arc. The sampling sites range in age from Pleistocene to Jurassic. Characteristic directions of magnetization of the samples were determined by the use of vector plots. Curie temperature determinations, thin section studies, and hysteresis studies showed that remanence of these samples is carried by fine-grained (pseudo-single domain) magnetite. Rotations reported below are measured with respect to the axial goecentric dipole field. The Plio-Pleisto- cene data set shows no resolvable rotation for the 22 sites. This data set suggests that the various terranes that make up the Philippine Arc have behaved as a single unit during the past 5 m.y. or that deformation has been below the limits of resolution. erpreting these results. Field and Laboratory Techniques A total of 550 oriented samples were collected from the Philippine Arc. These samples, which range in age from Jurassic to Pleistocene, were collected between 1981 and 1984. Samples were collected either by portable drill or as oriented hand samples. For most samples, the remanent magnetization was measured on a Schonstedt spinner magnetometer located at Kyoto University. Samples that^ possessed weak magnetization less than 10 -z Amp/meter (A/m) were measured with a cryogenic magnetometer located at the University of California at Santa Barbara. Alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetization techniques were used to isolate the stable magnetization from secondary magnetizations. For the sites that showed little directional change in the magnetic vector during demagnetization, three samples were demagnetized and served as pilot samples. If all of the pilot samples from a site showed similar behavior on demagnetization (determined by vector plots), an optimal level of demagnetization was determined by calculating a precision parameter  for each step of the demagnetization. cted sites. For many of the older sites, bedding correc- tions were required. Before applying bedding corrections, none of the reported sites had primary directions characteristic of the present axial geocentric dipole field. All of the Plio- Pleistocene volcanics and most of the late Miocene sites did not require bedding correc- tions. Most of these younger sites were charac- terized by magnetizations near the present field or reversed position of the dipole field. Interpretation of Paleomagnetic Results The results from Del Puerto suggest that magnetization was acquired after folding. The in situ direction is very near the expected magnetic direction for the late Cenozoic, which is consistent with magnetization during the Miocene to Holo- cene uplift of the Diablo Range, presumably in response to activity along the San Andreas system [Page, 1981; Aydin and Page, 1984]. The results from the sandstones and the lower-coercivity component in the calcareous concretions in the Wilbur Springs area similarly suggest magnetization after folding. The in situ directions of magnetization are near the expected late Cenozoic direction. The measured magnetization could be due to the Pliocene and Pleistocene volcanic and hydrothermal activity in the area. The normal magnetic vector at Jacoby Butte failed the fold test and the in situ direction is consistent at the 95% confi- dence limit with the Tertiary axial geocentric dipole. 145 Ma. These paleomagnetic poles from the coast of Chile coincide with poles from coeval sequences within the South American craton. Some of the igneous rocks that constitute these sam- pling sites crosscut a high-grade metamorphic complex that is distinct from other segments of the coastal cordillera in age, structural style, and metamorphic grade. This complex cannot be corre- lated with metamorphic rocks anywhere else in central western South America and could be con- sidered a potentially \"exotic\" allochthonous terrane. If this terrane has been added to the western South American margin, then accretion occurred prior to 170 Ma. INTRODUCTION During the last 15 years it has become apparent that the western margin of North America has grown and that the process of growth was related to the subduction of oceanic lithosphere [e.g., Monger et al., 1972; Coney et al., 1980]. crust of coastal Chile offers great promise of improving our understanding of the relationship between plate motions and continental tectonics [e.g., Dalziel and Forsythe, 1985]. The high-grade metamorphic complex described below is distinct from other segments of the coastal cordillera of Chile in its age, structural style, and metamorphic grade and cannot be correlated with metamorphic rocks anywhere else in central western South America (F. Paleomag- netic and radioisotopic data for mafic dykes and plutons that intrude this metamorphic terrane are reported here, however, and indicate that no significant rotation or translation of this part of the Chilean coastal cordillera, relative to the South American craton, has taken place since Middle Jurassic time. Some of the igneous rocks that constitute these sam- pling sites crosscut a high-grade metamorphic complex that is distinct from other segments of the coastal cordillera in age, structural style, and metamorphic grade. Virtual geomagnetic poles from 17 sites located throughout the central and western parts of the basin indicate that rocks of the basin were remagnetized after folding. A paleomagnetic fold test shows that the FisherJan precision paraxneter, K, decreases from 22 to 3 after restoring the beds to paleohorizontal. mite crystallinity indices show that the remagnetized saxnples were subjected to at least middle greenschlst facies temperatures, whereas magnetic blocking temperature estimates indicate upper greenschist facies temperatures. A K-Ar age obtained from clays of 1945 :!: 40 Ma (2or) is assigned to this metamorphic event. INTRODUCTION The Witwatersrand Basin located in South Africa con- rains some of the most thoroughly studied Arcbean gold deposits in the world; however, little is known about the thermal history of the basin. It is generally assumed that the basin was metamorphosed to no higher than lower green- schist facies [Tankard et al., 1982]. Constraints on metamor- phic temperatures are summarized by Hallbauer and yon Gchlcn [1983]. They argue that the maximum tempera- ture reached should be constrained between the inversion temperature of marcasite (157 ø) and the decrepitation tem- perature of the secondary fluid inclusions in Witwatersrand quartz pebbles (250øC). Volatiles are expelled from carbona- ceous material at temperatures above 250øC, so the appar- ently high volatile content in the Witwatersrand rocks also constrains this maximum temperature. Obcrthiir and Saager [1986] report that this regional lower greenschist facies metamorphic event occurred about 2000 Ma. This metamorphic age is inferred from limited isotopic evidence [e.g., Allsopp, 1961] and (indirectly) from the sup- position that the Bushveld Igneous Complex (BIC) is the most likely cause of the metamorphism. Until the present study, no

Obcrthiir and Saager [1986] report that this regional lower greenschist facies metamorphic event occurred about 2000 Ma. This metamorphic age is inferred from limited isotopic evidence [e.g., Allsopp, 1961] and (indirectly) from the sup- position that the Bushveld Igneous Complex (BIC) is the most likely cause of the metamorphism. Until the present study, no direct evidence for the timing of this metamor- phism has been published. Recent evidence points to much higher metamorphic tem- peratures. Phillips [1987] has reported that mineral assem- blages in Witwatersrand shales require temperatures in ex- cess of 300øC and perhaps in excess of 400øC (upper green- schist facies). A paleomagnetic study of this area should be able to help resolve this controversy by determining if the magnetization of the shales has been reset by a thermal event. It is generally assumed that the basin was metamorphosed to no higher than lower green- schist facies [Tankard et al., 1982]. However, Permian poles from the plateau and the craton appeared to be statistically indistinguishable [Gordon et al., 1984; Steiner, 1984, 1986] and indicated no rotation of the plateau. One explanation of the Permian discrepancy was possibly the lack of a well defined paleopole for the craton. Much of the craton data is from Peterson and Nairn [1971], who undertook a study to define the limits of the Kiaman interval. In so doing, they produced a number of Permian paleopoles. However, because their study was not primarily to define pole position, many of the paleopoles were calculated from only a few samples per formation. Other reliable Permian paleopoles were derived 2201 2202 Steiner: Rotation of the Colorado Plateau from the Rocky Mountain Front Range, a region deformed in Laramide time. These sites thus had the potential of being rotated; hence the relia- bility of the poles was unknown. The Permian problem therefore seemed to lay in the definition of the eraton pole, and a better defined pole was sought from a formation equivalent in age to a plateau Permian formation. Several paleomagnetic studies [Achache et al., 1982; Fagin and Gose, 1983; Mankinen et al., 1984; Scott et al., 1985; Renne et al., 1986b] have been undertaken in the RS in at- tempts to constrain the plate tectonic history of the terrane. ns and disseminated pyrite found in them. SAMPLE SITES Sample site locations are shown in Figure 2. Each site rep- resents a single lithologic unit except for site 14, where two different depositional units were sampled. Sites were chosen to encompass a variety of rock types and structural attitudes. The sites are distributed over approximately 3.5 km along strike, thus permitting the recognition of possible localized effects such as hydrothermal alteration, proximity to intru- sions, weathering, variable initial dip, slumping, or lightning strikes. Sampling sites were chosen to maximize the variation of paleohorizontal attitudes, which are shown in Tables 1 and 3. amples spanned the maximum exposed stratigraphic range of each sampled unit. Sites N-l, 6, and 7 occur in the Skookum Tuff [Scott et al., 1985], a densely welded dacitic ignimbrite. The Skookum Tuff is somewhat discontinuous along strike, ranging from 0 to 50 m thick, and appears to have been deposited onto a surface of appreciable relief. It is a dense, dark purplish-brown, ex- tremely hard rock that possesses abundant light-colored relict fiamme. Fiamme define a eutaxitic foliation whose orientation parallels bedding in sediments above and below the Skookum; the attitude of Skookum sites was measured directly on this feature. In thin section, densely welded vitroclastic texture is spectacularly well preserved, as are pervasive coarse devitrifi- cation spherulites and axiolites which are now composed of quartz and albite. Skookum phenocrysts are solely of plagio- clase (homogeneously albitized) and rare pseudomorphed mafic minerals (probably orthopyroxene or amphibole) now altered to chlorite and pumpellyite. Occasional lithic frag- ments comprise andesite and dacite. Microbreccia pipes con- taining abundant pyrite are visible in some outcrops; these may represent fossil fumaroles. Site N-11A is in a tuff' that resembles the Skookum in color, density, and extreme hardn

Controversy exists about virtually every aspect of the role of the RS in these various models: whether or not the RS is allochthonous with respect to North America, the polarity of subduction during its genesis, and so on. Several paleomagnetic studies [Achache et al., 1982; Fagin and Gose, 1983; Mankinen et al., 1984; Scott et al., 1985; Renne et al., 1986b] have been undertaken in the RS in at- tempts to constrain the plate tectonic history of the terrane. Each site rep- resents a single lithologic unit except for site 14, where two different depositional units were sampled. Sites were chosen to encompass a variety of rock types and structural attitudes. The sites are distributed over approximately 3.5 km along strike, thus permitting the recognition of possible localized effects such as hydrothermal alteration, proximity to intru- sions, weathering, variable initial dip, slumping, or lightning strikes. BAZARD Department of Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tuscon Paleomagnetic data from the Guadelupian (Upper Permian) Nosoni Formation of the Redding Sec- tion (RS) consistently exhibit two directional components of magnetization in addition to a late Quater- nary normal weathering overprint. Six sites in ash flow tuffs and tuffaceous sedimentary rocks, spanning 200 m of section, yield data that allow precise characterization of all components. Two additional sites in calcareous mudstones were too heavily overprinted to yield stable paleomagnetic directions. Thermal demagnetization of the tuffaceous samples in 16-18 steps between natural remanent magnetization and 660øC provides a detailed data base from which to calculate directional components. Together with previous paleomagnetic data from early Miocene rocks in the Kanto area, which is situated to the east of the Nohi area, the present results suggest that differential rota- tion of the eastern part of southwest Japan is attributed to the formation of northward cuspate shapes of pre-Neogene terranes which constitute the framework of the Japan arc. One probable explanation of the formation of cusps is a crustal indentation caused by the collision of landmasses on the Philippine Sea plate against the Japan arc in the middle Miocene. Thermal demag- netization (ThD) was carried out progressively in more than 12 steps up to 700øC. Specimens were heated in air using a noninductively wound elec- tric furnace. The stray field during the cooling cycle was reduced to less than 10 nT using a three-layer mu-metal envelope. Using the vector-demagnetization diagrams for progressive ThD of pilot specimens, the following sites were excluded from the routine demagnetiza- tion procedure: (1) progressive change of the vector endpoints did not show a straight trend. Secondary magnetizations were not removed effec- tively for this case, and (2) stable magnetic direction coincided with the present geomagnetic field direction before tilt correction. Such a component might be of the secondary overprint of the present field. The routine demagnetization was carried out on sites which survived the above-mentioned criteria. Eight to 12 specimens per each site were demagnetized at three to five steps. The ThD method was used for the sites whose secondary components were erased more effectively by ThD than by AFD. For the sites in which both ThD and AFD were able to detect stable primary compo- nents, AFD was adopted because ThD might give rise to breakdown of specimens in consequence of dehydration. The ARM has mean directions D = 50', I = +62* (k = 138, x95 = 5', N = 5 sites (23 samples)) for the Shawmere traverse and D = 23', I = +53* (k = 49, = 7', N = 8 sites (46 samples)) for the Racine traverse. Because of the high (>500'C) laboratory unblocking temperatures of the ARM in the Shawmere granulite-grade rocks, we believe this magnetization was acquired in early slow uplift, without tilting, from about 24-km to about 16-km depths, and has survived the later main KSZ uplift and tilting event. The Racine ARM has laboratory unblocking temperatures down to =400'C and was blocked prior to uplift from a shallower crustal level (about 8 km). With tilt corrections of 30* and 15', respectively, about the 35øE striking axis of the KSZ, the Shawmere and Racine A paleomagnetic poles fall on the Laurentian apparent polar wander path around 2.55 Ga, dating the time of initial uplift. Crustal tilting in the KSZ occurred after 2.55 Ga and was greater in the east than in the west. The B RM, found mainly in Shawmere anonhosites, has D = 115', I = -68* (k = 17, c95 TM 17', N = 4 sites (14 samples)), with a paleopole at 144'W, 49'N, near 1.1 Ga Keweenawan reverse poles and the normal pole

lift. Late Proterozoic 4øAr/39Ar ages from minerals with low Ar blocking temperatures [Farrar and Archibald, 1985; Hanes, 1985; Lopez-Martinez and York, 1986] suggest a mild reactivation at 1.1-1.0 Ga. Sampling, Measurements, and Analysis Five or more samples oriented by Brunton compass were collected from 15 sites on the Racine and Shawmere traverses. The eight Racine sites (46 samples analyzed) were in tonalites and mafic gneisses, while five of the Shawmere sites (27 samples) were in the anorthosite, and two sites (15 samples) were in gneisses of the southern line. Stepwise alternating field (AF) demagnetization to 100 mT and thermal demagnetization to 600øC were carded out in magnetic shields with standard commercial demagnetizers. Magnetizations were measured with Schonstedt and Digico magnetometers. The characteristic (highest coercivity I-Ic or laboratory unblocking temperature TuB) RM component, or ChRM, of each specimen was revealed as a stable endpoint direction on stereographic projections. Paleomagnetic and Rock Magnetic Results Three different groups of remanent magnetizations, which we call for simplicity A, B, and C, were isolated by AF and thermal demagnetization. Introduction The composition and structure of the lower continental crust have been inferred mainly from remotely sensed geophysical properties and petrological and geochemical study of xenoliths in diatremes and volcanic pipes [Fountain and Salisbury, 1981]. The key to a better understanding of deep crustal lithologies and structural relationships lies in the study of uplifted zones at ancient convergent plate margins, where erosion of the upper plate has exposed a cross section of the continental crust [Wasilewski and Fountain, 1982; Williams et al., 1985]. Such zones are marked by anomalies in seismic structure, gravity, and aeromagnetics, and typically have a gradational decrease in metamorphic grade away from major fault zones along which uplift took place. Copyright 1988 by the American Geophysical Union. Paper number 7B3042. 0148-0227/88/007 B-3042505.00 The Kapuskasing structural zone (KSZ) in north-central Ontario is believed to represent one of these crustal cross sections (Figure 1). The KSZ is a 400-km long, NNE trending belt of dense high-grade gneissic rocks, cutting across the E-W grain of greenschist and amphibolite-grade rocks of the Arcbean Superior P

lift. Late Proterozoic 4øAr/39Ar ages from minerals with low Ar blocking temperatures [Farrar and Archibald, 1985; Hanes, 1985; Lopez-Martinez and York, 1986] suggest a mild reactivation at 1.1-1.0 Ga. Sampling, Measurements, and Analysis Five or more samples oriented by Brunton compass were collected from 15 sites on the Racine and Shawmere traverses. The eight Racine sites (46 samples analyzed) were in tonalites and mafic gneisses, while five of the Shawmere sites (27 samples) were in the anorthosite, and two sites (15 samples) were in gneisses of the southern line. Stepwise alternating field (AF) demagnetization to 100 mT and thermal demagnetization to 600øC were carded out in magnetic shields with standard commercial demagnetizers. Magnetizations were measured with Schonstedt and Digico magnetometers. The characteristic (highest coercivity I-Ic or laboratory unblocking temperature TuB) RM component, or ChRM, of each specimen was revealed as a stable endpoint direction on stereographic projections. Introduction The composition and structure of the lower continental crust have been inferred mainly from remotely sensed geophysical properties and petrological and geochemical study of xenoliths in diatremes and volcanic pipes [Fountain and Salisbury, 1981]. The key to a better understanding of deep crustal lithologies and structural relationships lies in the study of uplifted zones at ancient convergent plate margins, where erosion of the upper plate has exposed a cross section of the continental crust [Wasilewski and Fountain, 1982; Williams et al., 1985]. Such zones are marked by anomalies in seismic structure, gravity, and aeromagnetics, and typically have a gradational decrease in metamorphic grade away from major fault zones along which uplift took place. Copyright 1988 by the American Geophysical Union. Paper number 7B3042. 0148-0227/88/007 B-3042505.00 The Kapuskasing structural zone (KSZ) in north-central Ontario is believed to represent one of these crustal cross sections (Figure 1). The KSZ is a 400-km long, NNE trending belt of dense high-grade gneissic rocks, cutting across the E-W grain of greenschist and amphibolite-grade rocks of the Arcbean Superior P

lift. Late Proterozoic 4øAr/39Ar ages from minerals with low Ar blocking temperatures [Farrar and Archibald, 1985; Hanes, 1985; Lopez-Martinez and York, 1986] suggest a mild reactivation at 1.1-1.0 Ga. Sampling, Measurements, and Analysis Five or more samples oriented by Brunton compass were collected from 15 sites on the Racine and Shawmere traverses. The eight Racine sites (46 samples analyzed) were in tonalites and mafic gneisses, while five of the Shawmere sites (27 samples) were in the anorthosite, and two sites (15 samples) were in gneisses of the southern line. Stepwise alternating field (AF) demagnetization to 100 mT and thermal demagnetization to 600øC were carded out in magnetic shields with standard commercial demagnetizers. Magnetizations were measured with Schonstedt and Digico magnetometers. The characteristic (highest coercivity I-Ic or laboratory unblocking temperature TuB) RM component, or ChRM, of each specimen was revealed as a stable endpoint direction on stereographic projections. nclusions The main results obtained in this study can be summarized as follows. 1. Folding of the Pont-Ran Formation is accompanied by the development of an axial planar cleavage. This indicates the occurrence of strain processes during folding. Strain induces the development of an anisotropy of the magnetic susceptibility. Strain and AMS tensors show a good correlation between their principal directions as well as principal values. We can thus consider that strain controls the magnetic fabric. Taking into account the presence of a pretectonic remanent magnetization, a strain-induced rotation mechanism is inferred for primary hematite that carries this magnetization. This mechanism is thought to be quite similar to the one described in the Maritime Alps red beds on the basis of X ray diffractometry measurements [Cogn and Gapais, 1986]. 2. The progressive alignment of hematite within the cleavage plane induces a rotation of net measurable specimen remanent magnetization toward this plane. At the scale of each homogeneously deformed site, this results in a deviation of the mean magnetization toward cleavage. A paleomagnetic investigation was undertaken to determine if this sigmoidal pattern was formed by kinking of originally straight photolineaments after the rock mass cooled below the blocking temperature. If the inner limb of the kink rotated 40ø-60 ø clockwise with respect to the outer limbs, then there should be a similar difference in the paleomagnetic declinations between the Florence Lake and Bear Creek areas. The paleomagnetic results indicate a clockwise difference in declination of 13.4ø+ 7 ø of the Bear Creek area with respect to Florence Lake. INTRODUCTION Although the Sierra Nevada batholith has been regarded as \"not internally deformed\" in tectonic reconstructions [Hamil- ton and Meyers, 1966], its crystalline rocks are cut by exten- sive sets of subhorizontal and subvertical fractures. The sub- vertical sets are recognizable on aerial photographs and are mapped as photolineaments [Lockwood and Moore, 1979]. According to Lockwood and Lydon [1975] the lineaments ob- vious in the air photographs are recognized on the ground as linear stream channels, long deep trenches, or parallel lines of trees and shrubs caused by concentrated erosion along closely spaced fractures. Lockwood and Moore [1979] show that de- spite local variations, a regional pattern of northeasterly lin- eament trends prevails over much of the Sierra Nevada. They note that the trends become more east-northeasterly from north to south and from west to east. According to Lockwood and Lydon [1975] the lineaments ob- vious in the air photographs are recognized on the ground as linear stream channels, long deep trenches, or parallel lines of trees and shrubs caused by concentrated erosion along closely spaced fractures. INTRODUCTION Our purpose is to reconsider the mid-Cretaceous paleo- magnetic reference field for North America. Such reference fields, expressed as paleopoles for cratonic blocks, fix the block relative to the Earth's axis of rotation and hence are essential in the study of the kinematics of accreted terranes. The study of the Cretaceous reference field began with the work of Runcorn [1956] based on three oriented samples from the Dakota Sandstone of Arizona, which yielded a paleopole in the Bering Sea (Table 1, entry A). During the early 1960s, more data became available, and it became possible to calcu- late mean paleopoles determined as an average of several rock units within a range of ages centered about the mid- Cretaceous. A remarkable feature of Table 1 is that despite the accumulation of new data and the variation in analytical procedures, the mean reference paleopole for the mid-Cretaceous of North America has remained little changed. Why then is a reinvesti- gation necessary ? There are three reasons. First, studies of mid-Cretaceous rocks in the western North American Cordilleran and in the Arctic regions are now very numerous, and it is becoming increasingly desirable to know the reference paleopole as ac- curately and reliably as possible in order to make accurate tectonic reconstructions. Second, the mid-Cretaceous is be- coming recognized as an interval during which widespread remagnetization of older rock units commonly occurred. Therefore a precisely determined reference field is required for accurate identification of magnetic overprints. Third, it is of great importance to determine the magnitude of the paleose- cular variation (PSV) during the mid-Cretaceous, when re- versals of the geomagnetic field were infrequent. To expand the paleomagnetic data base for northern Alaska, we focused our study on the Lower Cretaceous (Neo- comian) volcanic rocks and Albian sedimentary rocks of the Koyukuk terrane, as designated by Jones et al. [1987] and Howell et al. [1985]. Most of our samples were taken in the volcanic sections because we feel that the thermoremanent magnetization process is intrinsically more stable than the depositional remanence that is acquired at low temperature by magnetite-bearing sedimentary rocks and because thermore- manence is not prone to systematic flattening of the magnetic inclination. This report supersedes the preliminary results re- ported by Hillhouse and Gromme [1985]. c Rocks We examined thin sections of several representative rock types from the Lower Cretaceous volcanogenic sequence. In some exam- ples, such as the pillow basalt at site 5, the original plagioclase crystals have been replaced by epidote and calcite. The over- printing magnetization, which has dual polarity, was acquired after a Late Cretaceous orogeny left the region highly deformed. By fitting planes to tilt-corrected thermal demagnetization data and solving for the best intersection of the corresponding remagnetization circles, we separated the primary component, presumably a vestige of the original thermoremanent magnetization, from the overprinting component of the natural remanence. This analysis was successful because the tilt corrections of the sampled strata had sufficient variation to ensure a strong intersection of the remagnetization circles. Most of our samples were taken in the volcanic sections because we feel that the thermoremanent magnetization process is intrinsically more stable than the depositional remanence that is acquired at low temperature by magnetite-bearing sedimentary rocks and because thermore- manence is not prone to systematic flattening of the magnetic inclination.
